analysis.evidence: Abram takes Sarai, already identified as his wife, along with Lot, their possessions, and the people they had acquired in Haran. The next verb, וַיֵּצְאוּ (‘and they set out’), shows that Abram took them with him on the journey to Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with Abram as its subject.

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקַּח אַבְרָם, Abram is the subject of “took.” The verse identifies Sarai as his wife and Lot as his brother’s son. Haqor assigns the name to אבה through its אָב (“father”) element.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקַּח אַבְרָם אֶת שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ, Abram is the subject of וַיִּקַּח ‘took’. The marked אֶת introduces שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ ‘Sarai his wife’, the first definite direct object of that verb.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

evidence.note: The verse explicitly gives Sarai as the name of Abram’s wife.
God identifies שָׂרַי as Abraham’s wife and gives her the name שָׂרָה.
Kings and their noblewomen appear in parallel. The noun for the women, שָׂרוֹת, is the plural of שָׂרָה.

article.name: שָׂרַי
article.summary: Sarai is the name by which Abram’s wife is introduced. Her later name שָׂרָה has the same form as the Hebrew noun for a princess or noblewoman, supporting a similar meaning for Sarai. The text leaves the force of the earlier name’s ending unexplained.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for שָׂרַי linked to the שׂרר word family.
draft.definition: Sarai, the earlier name of Abram’s wife Sarah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:29 names Abram’s wife Sarai. Genesis 17:15 gives both names when God tells Abraham to call her Sarah.

analysis.evidence: In אֶת שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ, the direct-object marker אֶת introduces Sarai, and אִשְׁתּוֹ (“his wife”) identifies her as Abram’s wife.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The final י is part of the name.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abram’s wife before she was named Sarah.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 66585:4, 66577:3, 66561:4, 66324:3.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular construct noun with the third-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־וֹ.

evidence.note: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Terah’s genealogy names Lot as Haran’s son and Abram’s nephew. The passage gives no explanation of the name.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט with its etymology unassigned.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Lot as the son whom Haran fathered.

analysis.evidence: וְאֶת marks Lot as one of the people Abram took with him. The following בֶּן אָחִיו, “his brother’s son,” identifies Lot as Abram’s nephew, matching the genealogy in Genesis 11:27.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Haran’s son.

analysis.evidence: בֶּן אָחִיו means “the son of his brother” and identifies Lot as the son of Abram’s brother. The possessive suffix belongs to אָחִיו.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68121:12, 67845:13, 66581:1, 66568:4, 66568:12, 66562:3.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

draft.change: Add Gen.12.5 as an example of the existing definite-object sense of the particle אֵת at word index 0.
draft.definition: Introduces the particular person or thing a verb acts on, ordinarily a definite noun identified by the article, a name or a possessive suffix.
draft.evidence: In Gen.12.5, וְאֶת כָּל רְכוּשָׁם adds all their possessions to the objects of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.”

analysis.evidence: After Sarai and Lot, וְאֶת introduces the next thing Abram took, כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their possessions that they had acquired.” The possessive suffix on רְכוּשָׁם makes the phrase definite.
analysis.morphology: וְ is the coordinating conjunction “and.” אֶת is the unsuffixed direct-object particle.
analysis.sense: Marks כָּל רְכוּשָׁם, “all their possessions,” as a definite direct object of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.”

analysis.evidence: In כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their property that they had acquired,” כָּל takes the collective noun רְכוּשָׁם as its complement and denotes the full amount of their property.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add the root רכש and its noun רְכוּשׁ for acquired possessions. The source’s personal-name gloss does not fit this occurrence.
draft.definition: Property or goods that someone owns, taken collectively.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:5 pairs רְכוּשָׁם, “their possessions,” with רָכָשׁוּ, “they had acquired.”

analysis.evidence: Abram took כָּל רְכוּשָׁם, “all their possessions.” The relative clause אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “which they had acquired,” uses the same root to identify the possessions as what the travelers had acquired. The people are listed separately in the next phrase.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine plural possessive suffix. The noun denotes property collectively, and the suffix identifies the owners.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their possessions that they had acquired,” אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause whose understood object is רְכוּשָׁם, “their possessions.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew relative particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Append the verb רָכַשׁ with its Qal sense “acquire property” at word index 1. The source’s personal-name gloss conflicts with the verb’s form and its role in the relative clause.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:5 describes the property Abram took with him as goods they had already acquired.

analysis.evidence: In כָּל רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ, “all their possessions that they had acquired,” אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause whose verb is רָכָשׁוּ. The possessions are what they acquired.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural. The ending וּ marks the plural subject. The acquisition precedes Abram’s departure.

analysis.evidence: Abram took his family, their possessions, and הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן, the people they had acquired in Haran. The singular noun refers collectively to those who went with the household to Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ doubles the initial נ of the noun. The noun is common gender, singular absolute, and has collective reference here.

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן. Its antecedent הַנֶּפֶשׁ denotes the people whom they acquired in Haran and supplies the understood object of עָשׂוּ.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew relative particle.

draft.change: Add Genesis 12:5 as an example of the existing haran sense.
draft.definition: Haran, the place where Terah and his household settled on their journey from Ur toward Canaan.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:5 names Haran as the location of the acquisition before Abram’s household set out for Canaan.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן, the phrase בְחָרָן tells where the household had acquired the people. The following clause describes their departure for Canaan.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition בְ means “in” and governs the proper noun חָרָן.
analysis.sense: Haran, the place where Abram’s household lived before leaving for Canaan.

analysis.evidence: Haran is the point of departure. לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן gives their purpose, “to go to the land of Canaan,” and וַיָּבֹאוּ records their arrival there.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol in the third person masculine plural. The plural subject is Abram and his party.
analysis.sense: go out, depart from a place or someone’s presence

analysis.evidence: וַיֵּצְאוּ לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן means “they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” The following וַיָּבֹאוּ אַרְצָה כְּנָעַן confirms that they reached that destination.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לָ־ introduces the Qal infinitive construct לֶכֶת and expresses the purpose of the departure.
analysis.sense: go, move from place to place

analysis.evidence: וַיֵּצְאוּ לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן means “they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” כְּנַעַן names the territory toward which they travel.
analysis.morphology: Common noun of both genders, singular construct before כְּנַעַן, with directional ה marking the destination.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֵּצְאוּ לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן, Canaan names the land Abram and his party set out for. The next clause says they arrived there.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The directional ה is on the preceding word אַרְצָה.

analysis.evidence: אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן names the land of Canaan as their destination. Its first occurrence states where they set out to go. Its repetition after וַיָּבֹאוּ confirms that they reached it.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol. The י־ prefix and ־וּ ending mark the third person masculine plural, referring to Abram and his party.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 68613:21, 68383:22.
analysis.morphology: Common noun of both genders, singular construct before כְּנַעַן, with directional ה marking the destination.

analysis.evidence: וַיָּבֹאוּ אַרְצָה כְּנָעַן means “they came to the land of Canaan,” identifying Canaan as the destination Abram and his party reached.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun in its verse-final pausal form, with no prefix or suffix.
